visual.label: Score 6
visual.caption: 4 or above suggests possible delirium, with or without cognitive impairment.

visuals.title: Fix the cause
head: Cause
Treatment
rows: Review or stop anticholinergics, opiates, anticonvulsants

glossary.Cognition: Mental processes such as thinking, memory, attention and understanding.
glossary.Attention: The ability to focus on and follow a task or conversation.
glossary.Hospitalisation: Being admitted to and staying in hospital.
glossary.Anticholinergics: Drugs that block acetylcholine, such as chlorphenamine; they cause confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention.
glossary.Alcohol excess: Drinking above safe limits; both intoxication and withdrawal can cause delirium.
glossary.Seizures: Episodes of abnormal electrical brain activity causing fits or altered awareness.
glossary.Constipation: Infrequent or hard stools; a common hidden cause of delirium in older inpatients.
glossary.Inpatients: Patients admitted to a hospital ward.
glossary.Opiates: Painkillers derived from opium, such as morphine and codeine.
glossary.Peripheral: Outside the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Clinical diagnosis: A diagnosis made from history and examination, without a confirming test.
glossary.Cognitive impairment: Problems with memory, thinking or attention.
glossary.Infection screen: Tests looking for infection, such as urine and blood cultures, CRP and chest X-ray.
glossary.Urine culture: Growing bacteria from urine to confirm UTI and choose an antibiotic.
glossary.Medication review: Going through all of a patient's drugs to stop any that may cause harm.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: kidney function and salts such as sodium and potassium.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation or infection.
glossary.Chest X-ray: An X-ray of the chest, here to look for pneumonia.
glossary.One-to-one supervision: A staff member stays with the patient at all times to keep them safe.
glossary.Sedation: Using drugs to calm a patient.
glossary.Catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
glossary.Laxatives: Drugs that soften stool or speed bowel movement.
glossary.IV fluids: Fluids given directly into a vein.
glossary.Systemic insult: An illness affecting the whole body, such as infection or a metabolic upset.
glossary.Metabolic disturbance: An abnormality of body chemistry, such as low sodium or low glucose.
glossary.Acetylcholine: A neurotransmitter important for attention and memory.
glossary.Dopamine: A neurotransmitter involved in movement, reward and arousal.
glossary.Dopamine antagonists: Drugs that block dopamine receptors, such as haloperidol.
